opening.headline: When there are many places to defend but no standard on where to start, learn how to set priorities through attack surface and threat modeling.
body: LLM-based agents receive data not only from user questions, but also from retrieved documents, tool execution results, and connected external servers. If there are so many entrances, it's easy to try to block everything equally and leave dangerous paths empty.

In this lesson, we will first check why the model cannot distinguish between instructions and data, and the principle behind this is the context structure. Next, we'll look at what an attack surface is and what questions and classification frameworks lead to threat modeling. We'll walk you through the process of drawing trust boundaries on an agent diagram and sequencing defenses based on OWASP's LLM risks and Google's SAIF controls.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain attack surfaces and threat modeling procedures

This can be explained by the fact that it is difficult to distinguish between instructions and data because the model reads system instructions, user input, search documents, and tool results as one context.
You can prioritize threats and define minimum privileges based on STRIDE categories and ‘damage size x reachability’ criteria.
Can distinguish between user input, search documents, tool results, and MCP server trust boundaries

screens.title: There are many places to defend, but there is no priority.
screens.lead: Imagine an agent who searches internal documents, summarizes customer inquiries, and even drafts emails. When you select each entrance card in the diagram, examples of data coming into that entrance will be displayed.

visual.alt: A schematic consisting of an agent in the middle, four entrance cards, and a question banner below.

items.answer: This is text entered directly by the user. For example, a request to summarize this week's customer inquiries. It could be malicious or simply a mistake. Either way, this is the first entrance your agent encounters.

External content that agents find in their inbox or on the web and put into context. It may seem safe because it was written by a person, but it may contain sentences that read like instructions. It is important that this is how data that is not sent by the user enters the model.
This is the value returned by the tool called by the agent. Since the result of the previous call becomes the input for the next call, once the corrupted value is passed on to the next step.

An external extension that adds functionality to the agent. It's convenient, but the explanation and results sent by the server also go into the agent. If there is a server with more privileges than necessary, it can become a channel for privileges to leak.

screens.outro: There are four entrances and many more defense items. The question in this class is what to base on the order in a situation where time and manpower are limited.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: Think about each question in your head first. When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answers.

items.prompt: Where in my system can external people or external documents put data?
items.answer: It's easy to think of only input windows and API calls, but there are actually more entrances. Uploaded files, messages like emails, HTTP headers and cookies, and even values ​​stored in databases are all points of data entry. The starting point of a security check is to find all the points where data enters and exits.

items.prompt: When you were given a security checklist, how did you decide which items to tackle first?
items.answer: Often times, we start from the top of the list or fix the items that stand out first. However, if there are many items and time is limited, you need a standard for determining the order. The standard is to consider how an attack comes in and how much damage it causes, and the threat modeling you will learn later does exactly that.

items.prompt: Have you ever felt like the risks increase when you add a feature to your system?
items.answer: New features bring with them new entrances or new permissions. Connecting a tool to an agent increases what the model can do, and increases the damage it can do if something goes wrong. So the attack surface is not something you draw once and be done with. It's something that needs to be revisited every time the system changes.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize what attack surface and threat modeling tell us.

screens.title: Procedure for attack surface analysis and threat modeling
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what the concept is and how it works. The attack surface tells you where to look, threat modeling tells you what to do and how to do it, and the taxonomy tab tells you how to find and order all threats.

tabs.label: attack surface
tabs.body:
**Attack Surface** is any point at which an attacker can enter a system or extract data. To be exact, it is a combination of all the paths that data and commands take in and out of the system, as well as the code that protects those paths (authentication, permission checks, activity recording, etc.).

Examples of entry and exit points include:
- UI input window and form
- HTTP headers and cookies
- API, files, and database
- Message like email

Even though we have thousands of branches, we do not look at all of them separately. You can manage them by grouping them by type, counting them, and selecting representative cases for each type to check. You can also quickly scope things out by first looking at the two extremes: anonymous, unauthenticated users and highly privileged administrators.

tabs.label: Threat Modeling
tabs.body:
**Threat modeling** is the process of systematically finding out what threats exist in a system and deciding on a response, and is done by asking four questions.
1. What are you making?
2. What could go wrong
3. What to do about it
4. Did I do well enough?

The answer to the first question is usually organized into a **data flow diagram (DFD)**. A flow diagram depicts external entities, processes, data stores, and data flows, and draws **trust boundaries** where trust levels vary. Threats are primarily found in flows that cross this boundary.

A threat model is not a document you create once and close. If the system changes, the same questions will be updated again.

tabs.label: Classification framework and priorities
tabs.body:
To fully answer the second question, ‘What can go wrong?’, it is convenient to have a classification framework. A widely used framework is **STRIDE**, which divides threats into six categories.
- **Spoofing**: Pretend to be a legitimate user or system. Weakens authentication.
- **Tampering**: Change data without permission. It weakens integrity.
- **Repudiation**: Denies or hides an action. It weakens accountability tracking.
- **Information disclosure**: Data is revealed to unauthorized parties. It weakens confidentiality.
- **Denial of service**: Makes the system or data unusable. It weakens availability.
- **Elevation of privilege**: Gain access beyond what is permitted. It weakens the accreditation.

When applied to an agent, the path through which the instructions in the search document move the tool corresponds to elevation of privilege, and the path through which the summary leaks to the outside corresponds to information exposure. By entering the categories one by one, you can check whether any threats have been missed at each entrance.

The threats found are not all addressed in the same order. In theory, the order is calculated by multiplying the size of the damage by the probability of reaching it. Threats that are easy to reach and deal high damage come first, followed by threats that are difficult to reach and deal low damage. However, since it is difficult to accurately calculate the two values ​​and the effort required to correct them is not included in this equation, numbers are used as a tool to aid rough judgment.

Lastly, **least privilege** is the principle of ensuring that users and programs have only the fewest privileges they need to get their jobs done. Even if an error or manipulation occurs, the damage is stopped within that authority. This principle is an old standard that has been compiled since the 1970s in protection design papers.

tabs.label: the roles of the two
tabs.body:
Attack surface analysis shows **where** you need to check. It tells you which features and code need to be reviewed and tested, which high-risk areas require in-depth defense, and when the attack surface has changed and requires a new threat assessment.

Threat modeling determines at that point **what could go wrong and how to respond**.

Combining the two creates a basis for prioritization. The goal is to find all entrances as an attack surface, and use threat modeling to rank each entrance based on the size of the risk and response.

screens.title: Why can't models distinguish between instructions and data?
screens.lead: The figure represents the context and tool call loop that the agent reads at a time. Select the number markers one by one. A description appears of how system instructions, user questions, and search documents lead to an article, and how the model's output is translated into action.

visual.alt: A circular structure in which system instructions, user messages, and search documents are connected as one long bar and entered into the model, and the results of the model's tool calls are attached to the end of the bar.
labels: Context (what the model reads at a time)
The result is attached back to the context

markers.label: system instructions
markers.title: 1. Instructions written by the developer are placed in front of the context
markers.body: System directives are rules set by developers, such as roles, speech, and prohibitions. However, to the model, this is just text in context. It is not a setting that the server stores separately and executes in a special way. The model has learned the tendency to read and follow this text, but does not enforce the rules like a code.

markers.label: user message
markers.title: 2. User’s questions are linked to the same post
markers.body: User messages are immediately followed by system instructions in the same way. In conversation format, role labels such as system and user are attached, but for the model, the labels are also part of a token string made up of letters. The presence of labels does not mean that distinctions are enforced like grammar rules, but we simply learn to follow the priorities by looking at the labels.

markers.label: Search document/tool results
markers.title: 3. Texts from outside are also connected in the same way.
markers.body: Documents retrieved through search, email body, and values returned by tools are also attached to the context. Although the text was not sent by the user, the model does not know the source. If there is a sentence in the document that reads like an instruction, the sentence is read by the model like any other text. This is the fundamental reason why indirect injection through external content is possible.

markers.label: one token string
markers.title: 4. The model looks at the entire continued text and predicts the next letter.
markers.body: The model reads the entire context as a single token string and creates subsequent content. There is no separate input path to determine which part is instruction and which part is data. Researchers pointed out that the main vulnerability of injection and jailbreak is that the model treats system prompts and untrusted users and third-party posts with similar priorities, and proposed a method to learn priorities. This type of learning reduces risk but does not create grammatical level distinctions.

markers.label: Output becomes action
markers.title: 5. The output of the model becomes a tool call
markers.body: For an agent, the model's output can become a tool call request. When the model makes a call, such as sending mail or modifying a file, the code that runs the agent actually performs that call. Therefore, if any text in the context changes the model's judgment, it will lead to an out-of-system action rather than a textual error.

markers.label: retracement loop
markers.title: 6. Tool results come back into context
markers.body: The result returned by the tool is attached to the end of the context, and the model reads it and decides the next action. It is a circular structure in which the once contaminated value becomes the material for the next call. So, rather than expecting a single input filter to completely screen out all sentences, the basic logic of defense is to reduce the tool's power so that even if the sentence succeeds in deceiving the model, the tool's power is small and the damage is minimal.

marks.span: User input is text written directly by the user, which may be malicious or accidental.
marks.note: This is the first trust boundary. There is no reason for the system to believe anything written by a user. Regardless of intent, it is treated as subject to verification.

marks.span: Search documents are external content from the web or files, so there may be hidden statements that look like instructions.
marks.note: Data that is not sent by the user but enters the model context. The model has difficulty distinguishing between data and instructions, so sentences that cross this boundary should only be treated as data, not instructions.

marks.span: Contamination may be passed on as the value from the previous call becomes the input to the next call.
marks.note: The tool output, once contaminated, is passed on as input for subsequent step calls. If the value is not rechecked at each step, one boundary is effectively breached.

marks.span: Since the MCP server is an external extension, it becomes a source of threats and a conduit for privilege leaks.
marks.note: Content sent by the server can be a source of threats, and if the permissions granted to the server are wider than necessary, they can become a channel for leakage of those permissions.

marks.span: Manipulated output alone causes real damage
marks.note: OWASP LLM06 Perspectives on Excessive Agency. Once an agent has the power to call a tool, a single model output becomes an action, so the amount of damage is determined by the amount of power granted rather than the sophistication of the input.

screens.outro: Now that we've found all the entry points, let's organize the agent's own permissions and the risks posed by the components into OWASP topics.

screens.title: OWASP LLM Risk: Excessive Agency and Supply Chain
screens.lead: Select the two tabs one by one to compare the two risks outlined by OWASP. One is a problem of the authority the agent has, and the other is a problem of the components used.

tabs.label: LLM06 Excessive Agency
tabs.body:
**Excessive Agency** is a vulnerability where unexpected or manipulated output can lead to real damage when a model is given more capabilities than necessary. There are three roots.
- **Excessive functions**: Unnecessary functions can be called
- **Excessive permissions**: Operates with permissions that exceed the necessary range.
- **Excessive autonomy**: Executing important actions without human confirmation

For example, adding an extension that allows editing and deleting an agent that only needs to read documents would result in excessive functionality and authority. The same goes for plug-ins that should have been used and discarded during development, but are still connected.

Whether the cause of the malfunction is hallucination or injection, the result is the same. So rather than getting hung up on identifying the cause, reduce the scope of damage from the authority side.

tabs.label: LLM03 Supply Chain
tabs.body:
**Supply chain risk** arises from using components that were not made by you. Weak or outdated components weaken the entire system.
- Outdated or unmaintained packages
- Licensing risks of datasets and software
- Models that have ended support
- Pre-trained models with weak or hidden backdoors

Assets such as LoRA and PEFT used for fine-tuning and models running on-device also increase the attack surface. Externally imported models and adapters, like code, are inputs that must be verified for origin and tampering.

tabs.label: See also
tabs.body:
Both risks expand the attack surface in different places. The Excessive Agency's surface area increases the more power the agent has, and the more components the supply chain has.

Therefore, when checking the configuration diagram, we ask about both as well as the entrance. Does this agent really have the necessary functions and authority? And have you verified the sources of linked packages, models, and extensions?

screens.outro: While OWASP categorizes risks, Google's SAIF pairs risks with controls.

screens.title: SAIF Risk and Control Mapping
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation will appear. See how SAIF connects risk and control.

data.text: Google's Secure AI Framework(SAIF) describes AI system security through six key elements. It extends existing security foundations into AI, broadens detection and response capabilities, automates defense mechanisms, harmonizes platform-level controls, adjusts controls dynamically with rapid feedback, and evaluates AI risks within operational contexts. Controls are categorized under Data, Infrastructure, Model, Application, Assurance, and Governance, and each control is accompanied by a risk linked to implementation entity. For example, Training Data Sanitization is a control addressing contaminated or sensitive training data. Assurance and Governance is a control applicable across all risks and development stages. By designing controls to overlap with specific risks, Even if one floor is breached in the next layer provides mitigation.

terms.tip: This is a conceptual framework put forward by Google for AI system security. It shows risks and controls organized by category.
A control that filters out contaminated or sensitive content from training data. This is associated with the risk of contaminated or sensitive training data.
Indicates who implements which controls. Each control displays the responsible entity, for example Model Creators.
Control of inspection and governance category. It is common to all risks and development stages, not just one specific risk.

terms.term: Even if one floor is breached
terms.tip: This is the idea of a multi-layered defense. If one control fails, other controls are designed to prevent damage.

screens.outro: Now let's apply the concepts so far to an example.

screens.title: Explanation: The path that hidden instructions in the search document lead to the tool.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the attack path of the case step by step. Use the right arrow to move to the next step, following the entire path rather than just one input.

steps.title: Step 1. Normal request comes in
steps.body: Users normally request a summary of this week's customer inquiries. There is nothing wrong with this entrance. The person who requested it is normal, and the content of the request is normal. No matter how hard you tighten your input filters, nothing will stop you at this stage.

steps.title: Step 2. External document comes into context
steps.body: The agent retrieves documents for summarization and puts documents from external sources into context. At this moment, data that crosses the trust boundary reaches the model. This is the point where content not sent by the user gets mixed into what the model reads.

steps.title: Step 3. The sentences in the document read like instructions.
steps.body: Somewhere in the document there is a sentence telling you to summarize and send the results to another address. Because it is difficult for the model to distinguish between data and instructions, it may treat this statement as if it were a user request.

steps.title: Step 4. Model calls mail sending tool
steps.body: The model follows that sentence and calls the mailing tool. The results returned by the tool become input to the next step, so the contamination is passed on backwards. Now the problem is not text, but actual behavior. The moment the tool is run, the model's judgment errors turn into events outside the system. Please also remember that once an email is sent, it cannot be returned.

steps.title: Step 5. The amount of power determines the amount of damage
steps.body: The wider the sending authority, the greater the scope of damage. If you can send it to any address, your internal summary can go out. The key is not a single input, but the path from search document to model to tool, and the excessive functionality and authority that LLM06 speaks of increases the breadth of this path.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the route, let's decide where to cut this route and the order of defense. Since a single attack passes through multiple sections, there are multiple points where it can be interrupted.

screens.title: Commentary: Path-breaking control and defense priorities
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of adding controls one by one to the previous path. Select the next arrow to follow the order in which controls are stacked.

steps.title: Separate data and instructions at the document entrance
steps.body: We have a rule that external documents are marked as data and not treated as commands. It is a control that structurally makes it clear that content that crosses the trust boundary is a summary to the model and not instructions to follow.

steps.title: Separate read and send permissions in the tool section
steps.body: Tools that read documents and tools that send emails are not grouped with the same permissions. Writing or sending tools reduce the three roots of Excessive Agency by connecting them with minimal privileges that allow only the scope required.

steps.title: A person checks it right before shipping.
steps.body: There is a human verification point for outgoing transmissions. This layer prevents damage from being confirmed in the final step even if the model makes a mistake. It is also a control that reduces excessive autonomy.

steps.title: Set priority criteria
steps.body: Not all paths can be blocked with the same intensity, so we set a standard. If you start without a standard, only the most visible entrances will be heavily blocked. The path through which external content reaches and leads to writing or transmission permissions is first blocked. The path from user questions to a read-only summary is next. This ordering allows you to spend your limited time on areas that will cause the most damage first.

steps.title: Continuously update the threat model
steps.body: Each time a tool or MCP server is added, the diagram is redrawn and the four questions are asked again. Because with new entrances and new permissions, the attack surface changes, which can lead to changes in priorities. The key is not to assume that the order you decided on last month will be the same for this month.

screens.outro: Finally, we summarize what we have learned so far. Also remember why you stack controls instead of just one.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Let's connect the contents of this class into one flow. After reading, think about the last question for yourself.

paragraphs: This class started from the problem of having many areas to defend but no priorities. The attack surface is all the paths through which data and commands travel, as well as the code that guards those paths, and tells you where to check. Threat modeling establishes trust boundaries, threats, and responses by iterating four questions.

In an agent, user input, search documents, tool results, and the MCP server are each entry points with different levels of trust. Data that crosses boundaries at any point should not be treated as directed, and permissions should be reduced, whatever the cause, to limit the scope of damage. OWASP provides the basis for mapping excessive functions and authority, autonomy and supply chain risks, and SAIF provides a mapping of risks and controls.

The criteria for priorities are clear. Since not all paths can be blocked with the same intensity, limited resources are used first on paths with the greatest potential for damage. Paths where external content reaches and has write or transmission permissions are blocked first, and the threat model is updated whenever the system changes.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Decide for yourself which comes first: wide and thin at all entrances or narrow and deep at one dangerous route. In the examples in this class, also think about what criteria helped you make the decision.

checks.q: When documents retrieved through search contain sentences that read like instructions, what is the most fundamental reason why the model may not be able to distinguish them from the user's request?
options: This is because the characters in the document are longer than the user input.
This is because system instructions, user messages, and documents are all connected to one context and are read by the model as the same type of text.
This is because the model always takes precedence over the document when the tool calling feature is turned on.
This is because the document is encrypted so the model cannot verify its origin.
checks.explain: The model reads the entire context as a single token string. Role markers and learned tendencies help with precedence, but there is no grammar-level distinction, so we need to limit damage by reducing privileges rather than relying solely on input filters.

wrong.2: There is no rule that says tool calls take precedence over documents. Invoking a tool is the step that executes the model's output.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

glossary.def: It is a combination of all the paths through which an attacker can enter the system or retrieve data, as well as the code that protects those paths.
This is the entire text that the model reads at once. System instructions, user messages, search documents, and tool results are concatenated into a single token string.
It is a line drawn between components with different levels of trust. We focus on checking data flows that cross this line.

The principle is to ensure that users and programs have only the fewest privileges they need to get their jobs done. Even if an error or manipulation occurs, the damage is stopped within that authority.
This is a vulnerability that can lead to real-world damage when a model is given too much functionality, power, or autonomy, resulting in manipulated or unexpected output.
This is Google’s Secure AI Framework. It is a conceptual framework that pairs risks and controls of AI systems by category.

misconceptions.myth: The attack surface only applies to externally exposed APIs.
misconceptions.fact: Input windows, files, messages such as email, tool results, and internal interfaces are all entry and exit points for data. The internal attack surface is different than the external and some users may have high access privileges.

misconceptions.myth: Threat modeling can be done once at design time.
misconceptions.fact: A threat model is a document that you update along with your system. As you add tools or MCP servers, the entrance and permissions change, so you need to ask the same four questions again.

misconceptions.myth: As long as you defend the prompt well, the agent is safe.
misconceptions.fact: Whether the cause of the malfunction is hallucination or injection, the result is the same. Apart from blocking input, the scope of damage must be limited by reducing functions and permissions.

misconceptions.myth: The model reads system prompts and user or document text grammatically separately.
misconceptions.fact: For the model, it is all continuous text within context. There is a tendency to follow priorities through role marking and learning, but the distinction is not enforced, so the distinction between instructions and data cannot be guaranteed through input processing alone, and damage must be reduced through authority.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The model reads system instructions, user input, search documents, and tool results as a single context, making no structural distinction between instructions and data.
The attack surface is all the paths through which data and commands pass and the code that guards those paths.
Threat modeling repeats four questions to determine trust boundaries and responses, STRIDE finds threats and orders them by damage size and reach.
Search documents and tool results are input outside the trust boundary, and the amount of permission granted with least privilege determines the amount of damage.
With OWASP's LLM Risk and SAIF's Controls, you can base your defense priorities.
